length: 7 weeks · 11 lessons, a unit review and the CAT
description: Students learn how living things are told apart, named and classified, then follow matter and energy through Victorian ecosystems — food webs, ecosystem services and adaptations — before tracing how introduced species and human activity threaten biodiversity and evaluating how we conserve it. A Research Portfolio on the Eastern Barred Bandicoot is built stage by stage across the unit and is the preparation for the CAT, an Ecosystem Investigation on a species students have not studied.
notes: Every lesson carries a Caring for Country / First Nations perspectives slide with a matching booklet page — core, not optional (VC2S8H02).

achievement.text: Explain how biological diversity is ordered and organised, using classification tools including dichotomous keys; represent flows of matter and energy in ecosystems with food webs, and explain how changes in biotic and abiotic factors, including introduced species, habitat loss and climate change, affect populations.
Represent information with keys and models; analyse patterns; evaluate claims; construct evidence-based arguments from secondary data; communicate ideas for a purpose and audience.

Examine how people with different perspectives and worldviews, including First Nations knowledge, contribute to science; discuss the ethical, environmental, social and economic considerations of responses to a socio-scientific issue; analyse how science communication shapes viewpoints, policies and regulations.

descriptors.text: Similarities and differences within and between groups of organisms; classification tools, including dichotomous keys, order and organise the diversity of life

Matter and energy flow through ecosystems (food webs, food pyramids); populations are affected by changing biotic and abiotic factors, including habitat loss, climate change and introduced or removed species
Multidisciplinary endeavours draw on different perspectives and worldviews — the Caring for Country slide in every lesson
Proposed scientific responses to socio-scientific issues involve ethical, environmental, social and economic considerations
Science communication shapes individual viewpoints, community policies and regulations

Science inquiry — representations including keys and models (I04); analysing patterns (I05); evaluating claims (I06); evidence-based arguments using secondary data (I07); communicating for a purpose (I08)
Levels 5–6, consolidation — structural features and behaviours that let organisms survive (Lesson 8 adaptations)

prepare: Optional diagnostic: pre-unit check on classification.
Every deck from Lesson 2 opens with a 5-minute spaced retrieval warm-up.
review: Worksheet per lesson, checked in class; Stile check-ins; exit passes.
60-mark unit review under test conditions; the [Retrieval Quiz](quiz.html) (200 questions, filter by topic) for revision.
diff: Booklet scaffold boxes; Stile *Glossary: Classification and biodiversity*; glossary flashcards; *Handwriting Practice — Biodiversity & Ecosystems*.
Impact chains and food webs built one link at a time on screen; pre-drawn frames to fill in; sentence stems.
Before the CAT: the stage → CAT part map printed in the front of the Research Portfolio.
extension: Worksheet questions marked **Year 8 extension**; the *Above The Level* prompt in each portfolio stage.
The Year 8 extension parts of the CAT, banded separately by the rubric tool.

lessons.title: Living or non-living?
li: Name and explain the seven life processes.
Distinguish living, dead and non-living things.
sc: I can classify an object as living, dead or non-living and give a reason.
I can explain why fire is not alive.
explicit: [Lesson 1 · Living or Non-living?](deck1.html) slides — MRS GREN, dead vs non-living, Victorian examples

prac.name: Is yeast alive? — yeast with and without sugar, warm and cold, each under a balloon
prac.si: Write a hypothesis, use a control flask and measure balloon circumference every 5 minutes (VC2S8I01, VC2S8I02, VC2S8I04).
prac.su: Use evidence of a life process (respiration) to decide whether yeast is living (VC2S8U01).

guided: Issue the [Species Profile](species-bandicoot.html) and the [Research Portfolio](research-portfolio.html) — Stage 01

lessons.title: Classification — levels
li: Order the seven Linnaean levels.
Explain how features place an organism in a group.
sc: I can list Kingdom → Species in order and place an Australian animal into at least three levels.
guided: **Stile:** 2. Classification — a bee or not a bee? · 3.1 Levels of classification

lessons.title: Scientific names and the six kingdoms
li: Explain what binomial nomenclature is and why it is used.
Name and describe the six kingdoms.
sc: I can write a scientific name correctly and classify an organism into a kingdom with a reason.
explicit: [Lesson 3 · Scientific Names & The Six Kingdoms](deck3.html) slides
guided: **Stile:** Lesson: Scientific names · 3.2 The six kingdoms

lessons.title: Dichotomous keys
li: Use table-style and flowchart-style keys.
Construct a dichotomous key of my own.
sc: I can construct a simple dichotomous key for 4–6 Australian organisms.
explicit: [Lesson 4 · Dichotomous Keys](deck4.html) slides — worked key, then students build one

prac.name: Key the schoolyard — build a dichotomous key for eight fallen leaves and test it on another group
prac.si: Observe carefully, build a key as a model and find the questions that cause errors (VC2S8I04, VC2S8I06).
prac.su: Classify organisms by their observable features (VC2S8U01).

guided: **Stile:** 3. Dichotomous keys — how can we tell bees apart?
Fantastic Beasts or Aliens key worksheet

lessons.title: Australian ecosystems and biodiversity
li: Define ecosystem, biotic and abiotic.
Explain what biodiversity means and why it matters.
sc: I can explain why high biodiversity is generally more stable, and describe two Victorian ecosystems.

prac.name: Quadrat survey — species richness on the mown oval and a garden bed, three random quadrats each
prac.si: Follow a sampling method, average repeat quadrats and graph the two sites (VC2S8I02, VC2S8I04, VC2S8I06).
prac.su: Compare the biodiversity of two habitats and explain it with abiotic and biotic factors (VC2S8U04).

guided: **Stile:** 5. Biodiversity and food — how do bees impact biodiversity?

lessons.title: Food webs and energy flow
li: Classify producers, consumers and decomposers.
Build food webs and predict the effect of removing a species.
Describe photosynthesis and respiration as the two halves of the energy story.
sc: I can draw a food web of at least six species with the arrows the right way round.
explicit: [Lesson 6 · Food Webs & Energy Flow](deck6.html) slides — Victorian woodland species
guided: Lesson Book 2, Lesson 6 — [pp. 14–25](booklet/a5/Ecosystems_Lesson_Booklet_Yr7_A5_Book2.pdf#page=14), including the photosynthesis and respiration equations and the misconceptions box

lessons.title: Ecosystem services
li: Describe the four categories of ecosystem services, with Victorian examples.
Explain why they are threatened by biodiversity loss.
sc: I can sort examples into the four categories and give a specific Victorian example for at least two.
explicit: [Lesson 7 · Ecosystem Services](deck7.html) slides — native bee pollination, Caring for Country
guided: **Stile:** 1. Do we need to save the bees? · 4. Ecosystem services — why are bees important?

lessons.title: Adaptations
li: Define adaptation and its three types.
Link adaptations to habitat and niche.
sc: I can explain HOW an adaptation helps an organism survive — function, not just description.
explicit: [Lesson 8 · Adaptations](deck8.html) slides — Australian examples across ecosystems

prac.name: Beaks and food — tweezers, peg, spoon and straw collecting rice, marbles and “nectar” in 30 seconds
prac.si: Run fair repeated trials, draw a column graph and decide whether the pattern shows cause (VC2S8I02, VC2S8I04, VC2S8I05).
prac.su: Explain beak shape as a structural adaptation to a bird’s food (VC2S8U04).

guided: Adaptations Kahoot!; ClickView *Madagascar: lost worlds* with worksheet
review: Exit pass — classify three adaptations by type and state the function of one

lessons.title: Introduced species
li: Distinguish native, introduced and invasive species.
Explain the mechanisms of harm.
Evaluate management strategies, including their ethical, social and economic considerations (VC2S8H03).
sc: I can describe three ways an introduced species harms native species, and discuss one management strategy and its limitations.
explicit: [Lesson 9 · Introduced Species](deck9.html) slides — red fox and European carp impact chains

prac.name: The rabbit and fox model — a card simulation of two introduced species over 15 generations
prac.si: Run a simulation, graph two populations on one line graph and evaluate the model (VC2S8I04, VC2S8I05).
prac.su: Explain how predator and prey populations depend on each other (VC2S8U04).

guided: **Stile:** 7. Human impacts — are we a threat to bees?

lessons.title: Human impacts on ecosystems
li: Explain habitat loss and fragmentation, the edge effect, eutrophication and climate change.
Explain how threats compound.
sc: I can explain why fragmented habitat is more harmful than an equivalent area of cleared land.
guided: **Stile:** 8. Ecosystem dynamics — how are we impacting biodiversity?
Local case study: fragmentation in the Merri Creek corridor

lessons.title: Conservation and action
li: Describe in-situ and ex-situ conservation.
Evaluate strategies using Victorian examples; identify individual, community and government action.
Explain how science communication shapes viewpoints, community policies and regulations — e.g. how evidence about threatened species reaches the EPBC Act listings (VC2S8H04).
sc: I can evaluate a conservation strategy by stating advantages AND limitations, and give a Victorian success story with evidence.
explicit: [Lesson 11 · Conservation & Action](deck11.html) slides — habitat corridors, the EPBC Act, Victorian success stories
guided: Portfolio Stage 11 (feeds CAT Part F — the key criterion)
Zoos Victoria *Fighting Extinction* materials or a Landcare Victoria clip
review: Completed Research Portfolio checked — unmarked by design

lessons.title: Unit review
li: Retrieve and apply everything from Lessons 1–11 under test conditions.
sc: I can identify the topics I need to revise before the CAT.
guided: **60-mark unit review** — the old A4 unit booklet, [pp. 43–51](booklet/Bio_Ecosystems_Unit_Booklet_Yr7_8.pdf#page=43) (not in the A5 books)
Revision from the [Worksheet Booklet](worksheets-all.html) and the [Retrieval Quiz](quiz.html), filtered to the weakest topics
review: Unit review marked against the [Solution Set](solutions.html) (staff password)

lessons.title: Ecosystem Investigation
li: Apply the method practised across all eleven portfolio stages to a species I have not studied.
Communicate findings for a purpose and audience, using suitable formats and vocabulary (VC2S8I08).
sc: I can classify, map a food web, identify threats and evaluate conservation strategies for an unfamiliar species using a supplied species booklet.
guided: Reading and planning session, then the writing session
Parts A–G, issued with a Species Booklet laid out like the [Species Profile](species-bandicoot.html): Profile, Ecology, Food-web evidence, Threats, Conservation
